Items.Authors: Francisco Prada
Items.Title: The La Palma Quantum Interferometer: the next frontier for microarcsecond resolution in optical astronomy
Items.Abstract: The La Palma Quantum Interferometer (LPQI) aims to open the microarcsecond angular-resolution regime in optical astronomy. It achieves this by measuring correlations between individual photons detected by widely separated telescopes at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory (ORM). The initial deployment, LPQI-Pathfinder, will operate between the NOT and TNG, establishing a baseline of 550 meters. A planned expansion, incorporating the GTC, WHT, and INT, will extend these interferometric baselines up to 1.55 kilometers. By combining kilometer-scale baselines with a new generation of single-photon detectors and picosecond timing and synchronization, LPQI will attain angular resolutions down to approximately 50 microarcseconds. This unprecedented capability will enable transformative studies of stellar surfaces, compact-object environments, black hole accretion disks, neutron stars, nearby supernovae, and ultra-fast astrophysical transients.

Items.Authors: Samuel Day-Weiss
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: on-sky optical performance and characterization of the Small Aperture Telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO) Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) target measurements of the polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) from an observing site in the Parque Astronómico de Atacama, Chile, at 5200 meters above sea level. The primary SAT objective is to test models of the early universe by searching for a signature of primordial gravitational radiation, requiring high-precision measurements of the degree-scale millimeter sky. Consistent detector and cryo-mechanical performance over years of observations and precise measurements of optical systematics are critical to achieving the SAT science goals. We discuss the on-sky optical, polarization, and thermal characterization of three deployed SO SATs, each operating O(10,000) sub-100 mK transition-edge-sensor (TES) bolometers observing a 35 degree FOV through a rotating cryogenic half-wave plate polarization modulator.

Items.Authors: Matias Gonzalez, Vicente Coopman, Jonathan Antognini
Items.Title: AI Assisted Exploration of Dynamic Web Interfaces for Improving Test Reliability in ALMA Operational Dashboards
Items.Abstract: Modern observatories rely on dynamic web applications whose structure changes as users interact with them, making regression testing fragile and costly. This issue is relevant at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), where new operational dashboards such as the Integrated Alarm System (IAS) are being developed. We are creating a prototype tool that automatically explores a web application and observes how the interface responds to realistic interactions. It combines automated browser actions with AI-assisted analysis to detect interactive elements, group interface states, and identify unstable selectors. Early results on IAS reveal hidden interaction paths, structural inconsistencies, and selector behaviors that affect testing. This approach reduces manual trial-and-error and helps focus verification on unstable areas, with potential application to other observatory web systems. Integration into ALMA automation workflows is underway.

Items.Authors: Markus Gaug, Roberta Zanin, Michele Doro
Items.Title: In-the-field calibration of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) uses the IACT technique - where the atmosphere acts as a calorimeter of gamma-ray-induced atmospheric air showers - and measures the amount of Cherenkov light, which gets collected by telescopes exposed to the environment without a protective dome. Therefore, atmosphere and telescopes need thorough and timely characterization and follow-up calibrations.     We outline the leading contributions to these uncertainties and present a calibration plan that maintains the global error budget under strict control. We present the main methods to calibrate CTAO telescopes, including images produced by local muons and gamma-rays, as well as dedicated hardware that illuminates the telescopes with precisely known light intensities. Particularities of the atmosphere above both CTAO sites will be presented and means to monitor their components through a combination of publicly available data assimilation software, Raman LIDARs and stellar photometry.

Items.Authors: Laird M. Close, Jialin Li, Alan Alkhaddo, Donald W. McCarthy
Items.Title: On sky results for a solution for time domain follow-up in urban/suburban environments: light pollution minimization by use of new inexpensive NIR CMOS detectors
Items.Abstract: The Rubin telescope has created a severe problem for transient follow-up. Simply too many interesting transients and not enough follow-up telescopic facilities.  As low (and high) pressure sodium lights have been replaced by inexpensive LED lights the night sky in the visible (400-700nm) has significantly increased in brightness, while the sodium line at 820nm in the NIR (700-1000nm) has significantly decreased in brightness. We prove this with on-sky tests from a urban observatory (the Steward Observatory 21 inch, Tucson, Arizona) that observations across the visible (400-700nm) during new moon are 6.9x brighter in a light polluted sky (in units of ph/arcsec^2) compared to the NIR (700-1000nm) as measured with an inexpensive NIR sensitive Sony IMX585 CMOS detector (with a full correction for the 50% lower QE in the NIR). We will compare deep images of star fields and galaxies in the VIS and NIR.   Urban observatories can defeat light pollution by imaging in the NIR (700-1000nm).

Items.Authors: Imane Dazzazi, Martin Prest, Konstantin Stefanov, James Ivory, Douglas Jordan, Manish Patel
Items.Title: Proton irradiation effects on a substrate-removed Ga-free T2SL MWIR image sensor.
Items.Abstract: Testing image sensors under space radiation conditions is essential for assessing device durability and imaging performance for space missions. This paper investigates the impact of proton irradiation on the performance of a substrate-removed Mid-Wave Infrared (MWIR) Ga-free Type II Superlattice (T2SL) image sensor. A compact and transportable test system was developed to conduct in-situ cryogenic device characterisation under both dark and light conditions, at wavelengths from 1 µm up to 5 µm. This study aims to extract the damage factors of dark current and quantum efficiency, while also providing a comparative analysis with other infrared materials, such as HgCdTe and InAs/GaSb T2SL. The effects of irradiation on Random Telegraph Signal (RTS) pixels are also studied, highlighting the trap evolution with proton fluence in the Ga-free T2SL structure.

Items.Authors: Sandrine Juillard, Olivier Guyon, Jared Males, Garreth Ruane, Phillip Poon, Kent Wallace, Niyati Desai, Susan Redmond, Sebastien Vievard, Julien Lozi, Vincent Deo, Sebastiaan Haffert, Duffy Seamus
Items.Title: PSF subtraction using telemetry data: one more step on the path to reaching the photon-noise limit in high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: Current HCI systems are limited by residual starlight, which results in speckles in the final images, inhibiting our detection capabilities. Reaching the photon-noise limit in HCI is the next challenge for enabling the observation of fainter planets, ultimately Earth analogs. Standard speckle subtraction techniques using differential imaging (DI) can typically improve the contrast by two orders of magnitude, but offer limited performance at small angular separations where Earth-like planets are expected, due to strong temporal speckle variation and smaller differential leverage.  Using telemetry data is the proposed solution to better model and subtract the PSF. Wavefront information captured after the AO system correlates with the speckle pattern and thus can be used to predict the variation of the PSF. Using supervised cross-decomposition algorithms, we show that telemetry-based PSF predictions can achieve a gain of one order of magnitude in contrast compared to standard DI technique.

Items.Authors: Shunsuke Nakagawa, Ryo Hashimoto, Kei Sano, Takao Nakagawa, Victor Hugo Schulz, Necmi Cihan Örger, Jose Rodrigo Cordova-Alarcon, Yusuke Iwaki, Eyoas Ergetu Areda, Aoi Takahashi, Abdulla Hil Kafi, Raihana Shams Islam Antara, Kaito Hamada, Babu Vishwanath Hemath Kumar, Yukihisa Otani, Daisuke Nakayama, Akihiro Ikeda, Hayato Tanaka, Reynel Josue Galindo Rosales, Chinathip Narongphun, Isami Kato, Hayato Masuno, Emino Fukumoto, Chisato Arakawa, Shuji Matsuura, Kohji Tsumura, Yasuyuki Miyazaki, Ichiro Jikuya, Yuki Hirose, Koji Takimoto, Yuto Tome, Yuki Ohara, Akimasa Ojika, Yoshinao Yasuda, Hideo Matsuhara, Maiki Ebisu, Yusuke Ofuji, Risa Hirose
Items.Title: VERTECS: development status and system verification of flight model
Items.Abstract: The VERTECS mission aims to measure the visible Extragalactic Background Light (EBL), whose near-infrared brightness exceeds the integrated galaxy light by several factors, suggesting contributions from early-universe sources and intrahalo stars. VERTECS employs a 6° × 6° wide-field telescope with four-band photometry from 400–800 nm, a low-dark-current CMOS sensor, and a 3U bus equipped with the XACT-15 attitude control system, deployable solar panels, and a high-speed X-band transmitter. Developed under the JAXA-SMASH program since 2022, we are conducting its flight-model assembly and ground verification tests in 2025. End-to-end communication tests, long-duration tests, thermal-vacuum cycles, and initial-phase contingency tests confirmed system functionality, with several issues identified and corrected during verification. VERTECS is scheduled for launch on H3 Launch Vehicle No. 6, with all preparations for flight and operations planned for completion by March 2025.

Items.Authors: Casey T. DeRoo, Mallory Weber, Colin Packard, Philip Kaaret
Items.Title: X-ray quantum efficiency measurements of a low-cost, back-illuminated CMOS sensor
Items.Abstract: Complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) devices are a promising alternative to charged-coupled devices (CCDs) in X-ray astronomy, being (1) available at low-cost, (2) radiation resistant due to their active-pixel design (3) and operable at non-cryogenic temperatures with low noise. Our group has been evaluating the performance of the Sony IMX290LLR-C CMOS within the soft X-ray bandpass (200 – 1000 eV). We have previously found that this device has energy resolution comparable to the BI CCDs onboard Chandra, Suzaku, and eROSITA, and that the device survived radiation bombardment equivalent to three years in low-Earth orbit. Here, we report on quantum efficiency measurements of the Sony IMX290LLR-C CMOS within the soft X-ray bandpass (200 – 1000 eV) resulting from an X-ray test campaign at Beamline 6.3.2 at the Advanced Light Source.

Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: overview and current status
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object fibre spectrograph for ESO's 39-m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). It offers unique capabilities for a gigantic telescope in terms of multiplexing, wavelength coverage and spectral resolution. MOSAIC covers the visible (0.39-0.95 microns) and NIR (0.95-1.8 microns) wavelength domains, with medium (R~4000-5000) and high (R~18000) resolving powers. It has been designed to cover the largest possible area (~40 arcmin²) on the ELT focal plane. MOSAIC is optimised to achieve maximum efficiency for surveys, and to reach the best signal-to-noise ratio on the faintest sources, from stars in the local Universe to galaxies at the epoch of the reionisation. With its multi-object and multi-IFU capabilities, MOSAIC will be the leading tool for spectroscopic follow-up of faint sources discovered by major facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope, Euclid, Roman, SKA or LISA. This article presents an overview of MOSAIC together with the current status of the project.

Items.Authors: Ema Vo, Stephen Eikenberry, Anthony Gonzalez, David Smith, Harsh Mehta, Robyn Baumann, Kara Semmen
Items.Title: SMASHSpec: a testbed for actively-stabilized extreme  precision radial velocity spectrographs
Items.Abstract: Next-generation Extreme Precision Radial Velocity (EPRV) experiments demand stability approaching < 1 cm/s over years. Current passive spectrographs struggle due to long-term optical path degradation. We introduce the Single-Mode Autonomous Solar Heterodyne Spectrograph (SMASHSpec), a novel instrument using active stabilization. SMASHSpec achieves improved stability in a cryogenic vacuum environment with active path length metrology and thermal control. It features a cross-dispersed echelle layout for high resolution (R > 100,000) over a broad 380–930 nm bandpass. Light is fed via a single-mode fiber from a solar micro-telescope, using a Laser Frequency Comb (LFC) for calibration, targeting a few cm/s/year stability. Future designs will incorporate LISA-style interferometric Nd:YAG laser cavities for continuous, precise metrology to drive an active feedback loop, maintaining stability over decades. We will present the design details and progress-to date on SMASHSpec.

Items.Title: OPTIMIA: design of a multi-agent AI framework for diagnostics, control and operations at the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory
Items.Abstract: We present the design of OPTIMIA as a multi-agent AI "consciousness" for the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory, developed in a systems engineering framework. OPTIMIA is an observatory-wide microservice layer integrated with the global control system that fuses data from heterogeneous subsystems to support engineering operations such as fault diagnosis, incident prioritization, maintenance and performance monitoring, and the automation of routine engineering and operational procedures. The goal is to extend the effective diagnostic and operational capability of a small engineering team by embedding AI-driven support into the control architecture. We outline the proposed architecture, the main engineering interfaces, and the first pilot implementations currently being designed and deployed.

Items.Authors: Tyler J. Natoli, SPT-3G+ Collaboration
Items.Title: SPT-3G+: a cosmic microwave background experiment for the South Pole Telescope
Items.Abstract: SPT-3G+ is the next survey receiver that will be installed on the 10-meter South Pole Telescope (SPT) and will start observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) in early 2029. The SPT-3G+ receiver will feature 6,000 polarization-sensitive dichroic pixels (24,000 transition edge sensor detectors) and will improve on the mapping speed of the current SPT receiver by nearly an order of magnitude. This new receiver will produce an unprecedentedly deep CMB lensing map which will be used to remove or “delens” foreground B-mode polarization caused by gravitational lensing and reveal inflationary B modes. The SPT-3G+ receiver will observe a patch of sky overlapping with the BICEP survey for six years and achieve a band-combined map depth of 0.5 uK-arcmin. Together with BICEP as part of South Pole Observatory, the SPT-3G+ receiver will help achieve a measurement of σ(r) < 0.001 using data taken through 2034. I will describe the design and science goals of the SPT-3G+ receiver.

Items.Authors: Kyle D. Massingill, Bryan Butler, Brian Svoboda, Ricardo Crespo Vargas, Yoshiharu Asaki, T. K. Sridharan
Items.Title: Tropospheric phase correction using water vapor radiometers
Items.Abstract: I present on the development of calibrations strategies for the next generation Very Large Array (ngVLA). Temporally variable water vapor in the troposphere will introduce delay error to observations made with ngVLA. Calibration of this delay error is essential to ngVLA meeting science requirements. A water vapor radiometer (WVR) system is being developed for ngVLA. This system will continually estimate changes in the water vapor column density in the main antenna beam. The WVR system will be sensitive to the pressure broadened 22 GHz water vapor line in a variety atmospheric conditions. I give updates on our use of radiometers at the VLA site and on our approach to using atmospheric modeling to retrieve precipitable water vapor (PWV) from WVR observations.

Items.Authors: Arseniy Kuznetsov, Benoit Neichel, Sebastian Kamann
Items.Title: Hybrid analytical-neural AO PSF prediction using reduced telemetry
Items.Abstract: We present a fast, data-efficient hybrid method for modeling adaptive-optics (AO) point-spread functions (PSFs) using integrated AO telemetry. The approach couples a physics-based analytical model inspired by TIPTOP with a jointly trained neural network component. The model is calibrated and validated on on-sky data from MUSE-NFM. Validation shows high predictive accuracy of the model across diverse observing conditions, AO-correction regimes, wavelengths, and field positions. We further demonstrate the model's performance in a challenging real-world application involving source deblending in very crowded stellar fields.

Items.Authors: Irfan Kuvvetli, Ian Baistow, Leonardo Bernardini, Marco Carminati, Alexander Cherlin, Soeren Hauberg, Selina Howalt Owe, Ramsey Al Jebali, Dirk Meier, Christian Pommranz, Christoph Tenzer
Items.Title: i-RASE: intelligent radiation sensor readout systems for real-time photon-by-photon radiation detection
Items.Abstract: Intelligent Radiation Sensor Readout Systems (i-RASE) integrates physics-informed neural networks into the readout chain of a 3D CdZnTe drift-strip detector for real-time, photon-by-photon reconstruction. A custom low-noise front end, high-rate digitization stage, and FPGA-implemented ANN algorithms enable fast, accurate estimation of energy, interaction position, and timing, reducing reliance on traditional pulse-shape analysis. Laboratory tests show 0.5 mm FWHM position resolution at 662 keV, surpassing conventional methods. An ASIC under development provides eight analog channels with charge-sensitive preamplifiers, leakage-current compensation, wide dynamic range, and high count-rate capability. The architecture uses synchronized cyclic buffers and neural-state machines for efficient event detection. This proof-of-concept paves the way for compact, low-power system-in-package detectors for space-borne X-/gamma-ray instrumentation, medical imaging, and industrial applications.

Items.Authors: Riccardo Brivio, Francesco Guidolin, Matteo Aliverti, José Araiza-Durán, Iair Arcavi, Andrea Baruffolo, Federico Battaini, Sagi Ben-Ami, Alex Bichkovsky, Anna Brucalassi, Sergio Campana, Giulio Capasso, Enrico Cappellaro, Riccardo Claudi, Mirko Colapietro, Rosario Cosentino, Francesco D'Alessio, Paolo D'Avanzo, Sergio D'Orsi, Massimo Della Valle, Simone Di Filippo, Avishay Gal-Yam, Matteo Genoni, Ofir Hershko, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Marco Landoni, Luigi Lessio, Laurent Marty, Seppo Mattila, Matteo Munari, Giuliano Pignata, Kalyan Radhakrishnan, Michael Rappaport, Davide Ricci, Marco Riva, Adam Rubin, Bernardo Salasnich, Salvatore Savarese, Pietro Schipani, Salvatore Scuderi, Stephen Smartt, Maximilian Stritzinger, Fabrizio Vitali, David Young, Ricardo Zanmar Sánchez
Items.Title: A new automated scheduler for SOXS transient follow-up  observations
Items.Abstract: We present the Transient-Chasing Scheduler (TraCSS) at the ESO-NTT at La Silla Observatory for SOXS, the new automated scheduling software that will be used by the SOXS Consortium during operations. TraCSS is specifically designed to work with Targets of Opportunity (ToO) observations, with its flexible and fast-reacting capabilities. We describe its overall design, the scheduling algorithm and the automated night-management process.  We developed an efficient algorithm that can respond to real-time events and autonomously manage ToOs with minimum human intervention.  The scheduler is developed in Python 3 as a RESTful API using the Flask micro-framework and has been tested with real observations during the SOXS commissioning phase, ensuring an autonomous process of schedule creation, night management, and reaction to unforeseen events, always optimising the observations while respecting the priority of the targets and the night conditions.

Items.Authors: Giovanni Pareschi, Salvatore Scuderi, Andrea Giuliani, Stefano Vercellone, Gino Tosti, Teresa Mineo, Saverio Lombardi, Fabrizio Lucarelli, Giorgia Sironi, Nicola La Palombara, Giuseppe Sottile, Luigi Lessio, Andrea Bulgarelli, Silvia Crestan, Simone Iovenitti, Fausto Casaburo, Carmelo Gargano, Francesco Saturni, Ciro Bigongiari, Fabio Pintore, Fulvio Gianotti, Vito Conforti, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Luca Zampieri, Michele Buzzi, Rachele Millul, Giuseppe Leto, Christine Grivel, Edgar Molina, Josefa Becerra Gonzales
Items.Title: Completion and early scientific observations of the ASTRI Mini-Array air Cherenkov experiment for ground-based gamma-ray astronomy
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array, built at Observatorio del Teide in Tenerife, is a next-generation gamma-ray experiment that explores the 1–200 TeV energy range with high precision. It consists of nine 4-meter IACTs with dual-mirror design and SiPM cameras featuring a wide field of view and high efficiency. In 2024–2025, the first telescope (ASTRI-1) completed commissioning and began collecting data, including a 200-hour Crab Nebula campaign under different observational conditions. All nine telescopes are now nearly installed, with some already equipped with cameras, enabling initial stereoscopic science observations. These confirm system readiness and design effectiveness. The array's capabilities will allow detailed studies of galactic gamma-ray sources, monitoring of blazars, follow-up of transient events, and investigation of cosmic-ray origins. It aims to be one of the most sensitive gamma-ray instruments, bridging the observational gap between current IACTs and extensive air-shower arrays.

Items.Authors: Brandon M. Roach, Brenda Cervantes Vergara, Alex Drlica-Wagner, Phoenix Alpine, Ana Martina Botti, Claudio Chavez, Julian Cuevas-Zepeda, Juan Estrada, Guillermo Fernandez Moroni, Nora Hoch, Stephen E. Holland, Blas Irigoyen Gimenez, Agustín Lapi, Santiago Perez, Nathan Saffold, Javier Tiffenberg, Yikai Wu
Items.Title: Performance characteristics of thick p-channel skipper CCDs after proton bombardment
Items.Abstract: Skipper charge-coupled devices (CCDs) are an offshoot of standard silicon CCD pixel detectors and are capable of performing repeated non-destructive charge measurements, enabling deeply sub-electron readout noise. This capability has opened the door to single-photon counting from the near-infrared to the soft X-ray, making these devices strong candidates for astronomical instruments operating in the photon-starved limit. The p-channel architecture used to fabricate Skipper CCDs has been demonstrated to have an increased resilience to the space radiation environment. Building upon previous irradiation campaigns on room-temperature skipper CCDs, we describe the first radiation-hardness tests of p-channel skipper CCDs at cryogenic operating temperatures. We assess the performance of the floating-gate output stage and global CCD parameters. We find that these devices maintain excellent performance after displacement damage doses equivalent to ~10 years at the Earth/Sun L2 Lagrange point.

Items.Authors: Oren Ironi, Sagi Ben-Ami, Nicholas Konidaris, Joachim von Zanthier, Yuri Datii, Gerard van Belle, Elliott P. Horch
Items.Title: Sephira: stellar intensity interferometry with the MAST Array Telescopes
Items.Abstract: SII measures photon arrival time correlations between independent apertures to recover the squared visibility of the source brightness distribution. The technique is robust to optical path differences and allows offline correlation, presenting a promising path toward kilometer-scale baselines in the visible. We aim to demonstrate that with modern SPAD arrays and spectral multiplexing, SII can achieve competitive sensitivity with small telescopes. This opens the path toward Sephira, a modular, cost-effective interferometric array based on portable small telescopes. We describe the prototype design and initial laboratory results, and outline our vision for a future km-scale SII facility with flexible (u,v)-plane coverage. Science goals include rapidly rotating stars, Be stars, and interacting binaries, as well as sub-percent precision visibility measurements to characterize stellar surface structure and limb darkening, with direct relevance to exoplanet science.

Items.Authors: Gregory D. Wirth, Yun Wang, Massimo Robberto, Mark Dickinson, Thomas Greene, Jeffrey Kruk, Will Percival, Joshua E. Schlieder, Andreas Faisst, Lynne Hillenbrand, Jeyhan Kartaltepe, Nikhil Padmanabhan, Lado Samushia, Robert Content, Micol Bolzonella, Samuel Brieden, Lee Armus, Benedict Bahr-Kalus, Andrew Benson, Florian Beutler, Jarle Brinchmann, Hansford Cutlip, Emanuele Daddi, Kyle Finner, Jason Forsyth, David Glaister, Carlita Gorham, Andrew P. Hearin, Cullan Howlett, Jon Lawrence, Gregory Mosby, Eva-Marie Mueller, Sesh Nadathur, Kalina Nedkova, Zoran Ninkov, Ken Osato, Casey Papovich, Jack Piotrowski, Lucia Pozzetti, Alvise Raccanelli, Jason Rhodes, Shun Saito, Rebecca Schindhelm, Hee-Jong Seo, Zachary Slepian, Stephen Smee, Francesco Spezzati, Lee Spitler, Scott Streetman
Items.Title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
Items.Abstract: SIRMOS is a concept for a NASA Astrophysics MIDEX mission designed to revolutionize our understanding of cosmic inflation, dark energy, and neutrino masses by mapping the large-scale structure of distant galaxies with unprecedented breadth and precision. Leveraging the expansive Euclid imaging covering ~14,000 sq deg, SIRMOS will obtain slit spectra for 100 million galaxies at redshifts from 1 to 4 using a powerful multi-object spectroscopy capability enabled by a 2K×1K Digital Micro-mirror Device (DMD) as described in Robert Content's accompanying paper on the optical design. SIRMOS uniquely exploits Euclid’s deep near-infrared catalog for efficient target selection, collecting high-precision spectra (R>1300) with continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25-2.5 microns to eliminate gaps in redshift measurements and reduce systematic biases. By leveraging heritage bus and thermal designs, SIRMOS offers a cost-effective path to crucial cosmological measurements.

Items.Authors: Adrien Bolliand, Eloïse Bernaud, Michel Marcos, Eduard Muslimov, Manal Chebbo, Jiawei Liu, Gérard Lemaître, Jesús Aceituno, Stefan Cikota, Franck Agnese, Christophe Wabnitz, Samuel Boissier, Pierre Alain Duc, Emmanuel Hugot
Items.Title: Towards CASTLE first light: unveiling the low surface brightness universe with freeform optics and curved sensors
Items.Abstract: The CASTLE telescope first objective was to build a technological demonstrator to prove the curved sensor technology with real astronomical observations. Through its early lifetime, the project triggered the interest of the Low Surface Brightness Universe community. This presentation is about the status of the project towards the first light of the telescope, installed at Calar Alto, Spain.

Items.Authors: Arthur Vigan, Oscar Carrión-González, Gaël Chauvin, Benjamin Charnay, Silvano Desidera, Markus Kasper, Sebastiaan Haffert, Axel Potier
Items.Title: Closing the technology gap for the Extremely Large Telescope's Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (ELT-PCS): definition of science cases and expected science yield
Items.Abstract: The Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (PCS) is a planned ELT instrument aimed at detecting and characterising low-mass, low-temperature exoplanets with high-contrast imaging observations. The PCS R&D roadmap collaboration is now defining the main science objectives of PCS, developing the instrumental concept and deriving the instrument budgets, and analysing the scientific capabilities of the proposed concept. Two complementary aspects of this important preparatory work are 1/ the definition of the main science cases, and 2/ computing yield predictions based on instrumental assumptions and realistic population of planets. We describe the main science cases identified for PCS, and we show preliminary science yield estimates. We discuss the unique population of exoplanets that PCS will access, as well as the potential synergies with other instruments for a subset of those targets, which will be excellent cases for atmospheric characterisation.

Items.Authors: Arantza de Echenique, Paula Sierra-Sésumaga, Nerea Castro, Armando Bilbao, Bruce C. Bigelow, Eduardo Villar, Christopher Madden, Miroslav Vulinovic, Francisco Meza, Alberto Fernandez
Items.Title: BIM strategy for GMT enclosure design
Items.Abstract: The GMT Enclosure is a highly complex scientific facility requiring advanced coordination across disciplines and careful preparation for construction. This paper presents the implementation of Building Information Modeling (BIM) methodology during the design phase, emphasizing its role in enabling interdisciplinary collaboration and supporting the transition toward the tender and construction stages. The integrated BIM model served as a central repository of design and technical information, facilitating early identification of interface challenges and streamlining communication among international teams. Moreover, the structured and information-rich design model serves as the starting point for the tender and construction phases, in alignment with a design–bid–build delivery strategy. The GMT Enclosure case illustrates how BIM can enhance project readiness, reduce risks, and improve continuity between design and execution in large-scale scientific infrastructure projects.

Items.Authors: Fabien R. Baron, Daniel Johns, Stuart M. Jefferies, Douglas A. Hope, William O'Brien, Dmitriy V. Shcherbik
Items.Title: High-fidelity tomographic speckle imaging of scenes with spatially-varying point spread functions
Items.Abstract: We describe how a two-channel speckle imaging system can be effectively employed for high-fidelity imaging of objects observed under conditions where the point spread function varies spatially across the image We show that such degradation can result in false inferences on the target under study for two types of object: a high-contrast binary star system and an extended solar system planet. We demonstrate that our algorithms enable atmospheric tomography under D/r_0=20 conditions, assuming Taylor's frozen flow hypothesis. The layer heights are estimated via a grid search over the cost function. The spatially-varying point spread functions are recovered accurately enough to enable photometry of faint companions within the isoplanatic angle and across the full 40'' anisoplanatic Saturn.

Items.Authors: S. Marwede, C. O'Sullivan, A. B. Flood, D. Gayer, M. Piat, S. A. Torchinsky, E. Barbavara, E. S. Battistelli, P. de Bernardis, M. Bianchessi, F. Columbro, A. Coppolecchia, B. Costanza, S. Ferazzoli, L. Ferreyro, A. Fuster, B. García, M. Gervasi, L. Gomez Bachar, L. Grandsire, M. Hampel, G. Isopi, A. Mancilla, S. Masi, A. Mennella, N. Mirón-Granese, H. Ocampo, A. Paiella, I. D. Queirolo, E. Rasztocky, C. A. Rodríguez, F. Rodríguez, G. E. Romero, F. Sánchez, C. Scóccola, A. Solíz, A. D. Supanitsky, A. Vazquez, M. Zannoni
Items.Title: Performance of the QUBIC CMB telescope's detectors
Items.Abstract: The Q and U Bolometric Interferometer for Cosmology (QUBIC) seeks to find evidence supporting the Theory of Inflation by observing very faint primordial B-mode polarisation in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) using the novel technique of bolometric interferometry. QUBIC’s Technological Demonstrator, which has been commissioned in Argentina, uses 248 transition edge sensors (TESs) as bolometers at cryogenic temperatures in a quarter-circle layout across two application specific integrated circuits (ASICs).  The phonon noise equivalent power (NEP) of each detector is estimated by measuring the current response of the detector across a range of bias voltages at various bath temperatures. We conduct a long-term analysis of phonon NEP results to give an indication of the TES array's performance over time and the reliability of each detector.

Items.Authors: Brock Parker, Kelian Sommer, Aafaque Khan, Stephen Kaye, Erika Hamden
Items.Title: Read noise characterization and optimization of skipper CCDs using multiple readout electronics
Items.Abstract: Skipper CCDs achieve photon-counting resolution by implementing multiple non-destructive charge readouts, a property essential for ultra-faint ultraviolet observations. Our lab has developed a vacuum UV characterization setup for Skipper CCDs. We present the read noise of two 1278x1058 Skipper CCDs developed for the Oscura mission. We compare the read noise achieved with two different controllers. We perform readout sequence optimization, improving readout time while still achieving sub-electron noise, vital for astronomical applications. Through this optimization, we present read noise curves, detailing acceptable operating regions and parameters.

Items.Authors: Gabriele Coppi, Simons Observatory
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: Calibration of small-aperture telescopes with drone-based artificial source
Items.Abstract: We present the development and deployment of a drone-based calibration system for the Simons Observatory (SO) to meet the precision required for Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarization goals. We employ stable, monochromatic sources, capable of spanning all frequencies across the 90, 150, 220 and 280-GHz SO frequency bands, which are carried by a drone to the telescopes' far-field. This setup allows for accurate characterization of the beam properties, such as cross-polarization and intrinsic frequency scaling, as well as polarization angle calibration. Both of these aspects are crucial for the SO SATs to achieve their science goals. We summarize the results from two calibration campaigns for the SO SATs and discuss future integration plans for a dual-band source emitting in both the 90- and 150- GHz frequency bands.

Items.Authors: Alan Vasquez Soto, Nicholas Law, Glenn Walters, Mike Ronco, Hank Corbett, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Megan Dubay, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, William Marshall, Thomas Procter, Donovan Schlekat, Alex Bucheli
Items.Title: The Argus Array Conic Drive: an air bearing tracking system for large telescope arrays
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is the first large optical telescope array, monitoring 8,000 square degrees simultaneously with 1,200 individual 28-cm telescopes tracking the sky as a monolithic 8m-class system. The Conic Drive is similar to an equatorial platform, with geometry optimized for the Argus Array to achieve <1 arcsecond pointing drift over 3-degree tracking ratchets with <0.35 arcseconds RMS tracking error. Porous media air bearings enable this tracking performance by eliminating conventional bearing runout while providing high stiffness and zero friction. We developed alignment procedures and validation methods using precision tilt sensors and specialized jigs to ensure tracking stability. We will present tracking system mechanical design, air bearing performance characterization, alignment procedures, and initial results from in-lab testing.

Items.Authors: Emiliano Cordelli, Ernesto Dölling, Dora Föhring, Pablo Ramirez-Moreta, Luca Conversi, Peter Droll, Johannes Klug, Richard Moissl, Vanshika Agrawal, Francisco Ocana, Marta Cametti, Elmar Brendel
Items.Title: From commissioning to operations: testing Europe’s next-generation NEO survey telescope Flyeye 1
Items.Abstract: The Flyeye 1 telescope marks a major step in Europe’s planetary defence, introducing a new multi-aperture design for wide-field NEO detection. To ensure operational readiness, an extensive end-to-end testing campaign was conducted. This paper outlines the preoperational validation approach, covering optical alignment, detector calibration, and full DPC verification under realistic environmental conditions. Robustness of the DPC was assessed using simulated and real-sky datasets. Integration tests addressed hardware–software interoperability, autonomous scheduling, real-time image processing, and compatibility with ESA’s NEOCC. Additional challenges included site preparation, network connectivity, and commissioning under variable atmospheric conditions. The outcomes of this end-to-end testing campaign define the roadmap toward full operational capability and inform for future deployments, ensuring the reliability and resilience of Europe’s planetary defence infrastructure.

Items.Authors: Nathan Bush, Michael E. Hoenk, April Jewell, Charles Shapiro, Shouleh Nikzad
Items.Title: Impact of Irradiation Temperature on CMOS Imager Performance: A Comparative Study of Cryogenic and Room Temperature Degradation in the CIS120
Items.Abstract: For space-based precision astronomy measurements it is now well understood that the most accurate estimate of performance degradation comes from irradiation of sensors at the nominal operating temperature of the mission. While many studies on these differences exist for CCDs, information on CMOS remains comparably limited. In this study, two Teledyne-e2v CIS120s were irradiated with protons to 5.0E10 p/cm2 (10 MeV equiv.) at both 203 K and at room temperature, and two additional devices were irradiated to 30 krad using a Co-60 γ source at the same temperatures. We compare and contrast degradation from each irradiation at each temperature, with a particular focus on dark current, charge transfer effects, flat-band shifts and Quantum Efficiency from the UV through the visible.

Items.Authors: Harry-Dean Kenchington-Goldsmith, Nemanja Jovanovic, Anusha J. Pai Asnodkar, Sanny Ahmed, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Pierre Labeye, Michael Ireland, Stephen Madden
Items.Title: Technologies and novel components for broadband splitting and coupling in interferometry, including pairwise coupling and nulling interferometry
Items.Abstract: Photonics enables the replacement of large bulk-optic assemblies with compact, monolithic photonic chips. Recent advances in mid-IR, near-IR, and visible photonics have accelerated their use in interferometric instrumentation, as demonstrated by GRAVITY and NOTT at the VLTI and FIRST and GLINT at Subaru. Future photonic systems will require more complex circuits capable of preprocessing light on chip while maintaining stability, compactness, and broadband performance. High-index-contrast planar platforms offer sub-wavelength waveguides with strong scalability for ground-based facilities and high functional density for space missions. This work highlights materials and photonic components that provide broadband splitting and coupling across the astronomical J- and H-bands, enabling next-generation interferometry and nulling interferometry.

Items.Authors: Sean MacBride, Lynne Jones, Peter Yoachim, Tiago Ribeiro, Leanne Guy, Shreya Anand, Erin Howard, Ian Sullivan, David Wang, Eric Bellm, Robert Armstrong, Michael Wood-Vasey, Alex Drlica-Wagner, Kenneth Herner, Gautham Narayan, Tatiana A. Cuellar, Federica Bianco, Bruno Sánchez, John Banovetz, Anastasia Alexov, Erik Dennihy, Robert Blum, Yousuke Utsumi, Robert Lupton, Keith Bechtol, Zeljko Ivezic, Kris Mortensen, Paulina Venegas Salas, Yijung Kang, Alysha Shugart, Narayan Khadka, Kshitija Kelkar, Danica Zilkova, Kevin Fanning, Chris Walter, Chris Weaver, Fabian Araneda-Baltierra, Igor Andreoni, Andreja Gomboc, Marcelle Soares-Santos, Pedro Bernardinelli, Colin Chandler, Devanshi Singh
Items.Title: The Rubin Observatory target-of-opportunity program in the first year of operations
Items.Abstract: Rubin Observatory is designed for rapid discovery, enabling the identification of rare and fast-evolving astrophysical transients more quickly than any existing facility. Three percent of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time is reserved for Target of Opportunity (ToO) observations, supporting rapid responses to gravitational-wave sources, high-energy neutrinos, hazardous asteroids, and other events. Because ToO observations operate outside standard LSST cadence, they require dedicated planning to maximize scientific return. This work reviews community-developed ToO strategies, integration efforts during Rubin’s first year of operations, the ToO events pursued since Rubin first light, and the overall efficiency of the ToO response system.

Items.Authors: Rinon Kageyama, Kohji Tsumura, Hideo Matsuhara, Daisuke Yonetoku, Akihiro Doi, Akihiro Miyasaka, Shuji Matsuura, Hiroshi Akitaya, Koji S. Kawabata
Items.Title: Thermal analysis of the optical and near-infrared telescope (MONSTER) on board the HiZ-GUNDAM satellite
Items.Abstract: HiZ-GUNDAM aims to explore the early Universe and advance multi-messenger astrophysics through rapid detection of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The MONSTER near-infrared telescope performs five-band imaging from 0.5 to 2.5 µm of GRBs detected by the wide-field X-ray monitor EAGLE and provides photometric redshifts. To ensure high sensitivity, the telescope body and HgCdTe detector must be cooled below 200 K and 120 K by radiative cooling. After GRB detection, the satellite slews toward the GRB, increasing thermal input. We evaluated the thermal worst-case condition, defined as the attitude with maximum heat load at the hottest point, and established a method to compute satellite attitude using rotation matrices based on the Sun’s right ascension and declination. Thermal analysis shows that even in the worst case, the telescope body and detector remain at 171 K and 106 K. In this presentation, we report the development and thermal assessment of the MONSTER telescope onboard HiZ-GUNDAM.

Items.Authors: Rikke Stougaard Klausen, Irfan Kuvvetli, Selina R. H. Owe, Michał Kossakowski, Denis Tcherniak, Alexander Cherlin, Carl Budtz-Jørgensen, Guillermo B. Guinea
Items.Title: Next-generation 3D CdZnTe matrix detector with reduced noise and minimal readout requirements
Items.Abstract: Accurate and compact radiation detectors are increasingly needed in MeV space missions, yet current semiconductor technologies are limited by electronic noise, capacitance, and system complexity. We present a next-generation 3D CZT Matrix Detector that uses a novel fine pitch electrode geometry to significantly reduce electronic noise and pixel capacitance. By optimizing weighting fields and charge sharing behavior, the design enhances signal fidelity and supports superior spatial and energy resolution at room temperature. Our approach combines 3D charge transport and field simulations with experimental studies that are used to validate detector performance.     A key advantage of the electrode geometry is that it extracts complete radiation information with very few readout channels, reducing detector size, mass, and power - making the system well suited for space missions.

Items.Authors: Douglas A. Hope, Fabien Baron, Stuart M. Jefferies, Dmitriy V. Shcherbik, Lexi Azoulay, Jeffrey Kuhn
Items.Title: Non-coronagraphic PSF engineering
Items.Abstract: We propose non-coronagraphic PSF engineering to create dark regions in the image without eliminating the flux from the primary star. These dual measurements of the host and the secondary system would allow for their characterization. Second, we investigate the achievable contrast levels with this PSF engineering approach for broadband imaging and study the achievable spectral resolution of the targets. Our approach considers full-aperture systems such as the Keck, TMT, GMT, and a proposed Fizeau imaging telescope called the Exo-Life Finder. We will report on the achievable contrast and spectral resolution from numerical and optical experiments that use deformable mirrors to perform phase manipulation and engineer PSFs with a dark region

R. Gallazzi, M. Guarcello, L. Izzo, F. La Barbera, C. Lardo, M. Longhetti, A. Longobardo, L. Magrini, C. Mancini, A. Mura, E. Piconcelli, A. Pizzella, L. Podio, M. Polletta, L. Prisinzano, F. Ricci, V. Ripepi, V. Roccatagliata, E. Vanzella, G. Vietri, H. Wang
Items.Title: SHARP: a spectrograph proposal to fully exploit ELT capabilities and look beyond JWST
Items.Abstract: The Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), with their large apertures and cutting-edge Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) systems, promise to deliver data sharper and deeper than even the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). SHARP is a concept study for a near-IR (0.95–2.45 $\mu$m) spectrograph specifically designed to fully exploit the collecting area and angular resolution capabilities of the upcoming ESO's ELT. The instrument concept is driven by the goal of tackling the most important questions in astrophysics and cosmology. This requires versatility to accommodate diverse observational needs. SHARP (http://sharp.brera.inaf.it) is composed of two main units: NEXUS, a Multi-Object Spectrograph and VESPER, a multi-Integral Field Unit. This presentation provides an overview of the science behind SHARP, its optical design and capabilities, as well as the project itself.

Items.Authors: Toby Duffy, David Brodrick, Jesse Cranney, Nian Jiang, François Rigaut, Naomi McClure-Griffiths, Jason Li
Items.Title: AstroRAG: a practical application of retrieval-augmented generation for documentation-driven astronomy projects
Items.Abstract: Large astronomical instrumentation projects such as MAVIS and the SKA produce large volumes of documentation. While these documents are essential to effective project delivery and long-term operations, their scale and distribution make it increasingly difficult for teams to efficiently search, interpret, and reuse existing information.    This paper describes the use of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques applied to bulk project documentation for complex astronomical instruments, including MAVIS and the SKA. Rather than focusing on algorithmic performance, the emphasis is on practical deployment and use within real projects, including document ingestion, grounding of responses in authoritative source material, and alignment with established engineering and science workflows.

Items.Authors: Sofia Savorgnano, Andrea Catalano, Juan Francisco Macias Perez, Julien Bounmy, Olivier Bourrion, Martino Calvo, Olivier Choulet, Gregory Garde, Anne Gerardin, Mile Kusulja, Alessandro Monfardini, Nicolas Ponthieu, Damien Tourres, Francis Vezzu
Items.Title: High-precision polarization measurements with LEKIDs
Items.Abstract: We present recent laboratory results on LEKID arrays optimized for high-precision millimeter-wave polarimetry. Using a dedicated cryogenic test bench at LPSC—combining a sky simulator with photometric and polarized sources—we characterized the electrical, photometric, spectroscopic, and polarization performance of the detectors. Key metrics include responsivity, NEP, bandpass, beam properties, and polarization-angle reconstruction. The arrays achieve ∼0.1° precision with strong control of systematics, meeting the requirements of next-generation CMB polarization experiments and demonstrating the potential of this filled-array LEKID configuration for future cosmological applications.

Items.Authors: Vinand Prayag, Nivedita Mahesh, Gregg Hallinan, Yanfen Lin, Judd Bowman, Mike Virgin, Charlie Harnach, Mark Hodges, Joseph Lazio
Items.Title: Measurement of all-sky neutral hydrogen absorption spectrum (MANAS)

Items.Authors: Fabio Tenegi Sanginés, Félix Gracia, Afrodisio Vega-Moreno
Items.Title: SLA-AM Optical Elements for application in Astronomical Instrumentation
Items.Abstract: Additive Manufacture (AM) comprises a group of technologies that allow to go from a 3D model to manufactured components, creating them layer by layer until the part is complete. Among the advantages of AM, the ones that apply most to astronomical instrumentation are part complexity and consolidation, the addition of functionalities, design freedom and lightweighting capability.  The aim of this talk is to present the studies carried out within the IAC's Mechanical Engineering Department for the development of optical elements made in SLA technology and applicable to Astronomical Instruments. These studies include both optical and mechanical properties, as well as vacuum compatibility, etc.

Items.Authors: Jonah T. Hansen, Thomas Birbacher, Germain Garreau, Julio Pino Jiménez, Emilie Bouzerand, Felix A. Dannert, David Eglin, Lee Feinberg, Adrian M. Glauser, Maximillian Kirchhoff, Oliver Pitz, Eckhart Spalding, Sascha P. Quanz
Items.Title: A NICE (Nulling Interferometry Cryogenic Experiment) update: beyond 1e-5 and towards cryogenic operation
Items.Abstract: The Nulling Interferometry Cryogenic Experiment (NICE) is a mid-infrared laboratory testbed at ETH Zurich  that aims to not only reproduce the deep (<1e−5) broadband nulls of the nulling testbeds of the early 2000s,  but also at the required sensitivity levels expected for the LIFE space mission. This sensitivity enforces the  experiment to go cryogenic at temperatures around 15 K; an ambitious task for an ultra-precise interferometer.  We share our results of the ambient precursor experiment, demonstrating repeatable < 1e−5 nulls at a single  wavelength and high throughput, and investigations into the nulling performance across a broader bandpass and  with dual polarisation states. We will also highlight the push towards cryogenic operation, with the instalment  of a new 15 K test cryostat that will inform our choices of materials and optomechanical mounting techniques

Items.Authors: Michael J. Freyberg, Norbert Meidinger, Michael Smith, Emanuele Perinati
Items.Title: Long-term evolution of micrometeoroid impact effects in pnCCDs (EPIC-pn, eROSITA)
Items.Abstract: Impacts of micro-meteoroids as micron-sized dust particles at hypervelocities onto X-ray astromonmical CCDs in space can cause performance degradation but also lead to fatal failures.  Here we report on the 3 impacts onto the pn-CCDs of XMM-Newton (EPIC-pn camera) and the 7 onto eROSITA aboard Spectum-Roentgen-Gamma.  We analyze in detail the long-term evolution of the damage effects in these back-illuminated silicon devices.  We discuss the presence and absence of associated optical flashes.

Items.Authors: Jianan Cong, Zhengyang Li, Xiaoyan Li
Items.Title: System design of the wide-field near-infrared telescope at Dome A, Antarctica, and first daytime near-infrared observations
Items.Abstract: Dome A in Antarctica likely has the best observing conditions on the Earth's surface in the near-infrared owing to its sky-light background and superior seeing conditions. This work introduces the system design of the first wide field-of-view near-infrared telescope at Dome A. We present the telescope’s optical system as well as the design of the direct-drive motor mount and mechanical defrosting system capable of withstanding the extreme Antarctic environment. Through this project, we validated the key technologies described above and achieved the first daytime J-band bright-star observations during the Antarctic summer. Stars as faint as J- 10.06 mag were significantly detected with an effective exposure time of 175 s around midnight.

Items.Authors: James H. Tutt, Bruce Lairson, Jeffrey De Lucca, Alexandra Higley, Ross McCurdy, Randall L. McEntaffer, Drew M. Miles, Keith Rice
Items.Title: Testing of SiC grid-based blocking filters to increase their technology readiness level
Items.Abstract: Progress over the past year has advanced mitigation of contamination buildup on cold focal-plane detectors using free-standing, actively heated blocking filters. Development, fabrication, and environmental testing of large-format SiC support grids have continued, enabling room-temperature X-ray filters with minimal power. Multiple square-grid designs suitable for the AXIS mission have been produced and mechanically tested, including vibration evaluations for launch survivability. Thermal-vacuum experiments have mapped steady-state and transient temperature behavior, refining power-budget models for reheating under radiative cooling. Next steps include additional vibration tests, long-duration thermal-vacuum cycles, and studies of filter thermal conductivity to further raise TRL. These results position SiC room-temperature blocking filters as a strong solution for future missions requiring contamination control and thermal efficiency.

Items.Authors: Jessica A. Gaskin, Julie A. Crooke
Items.Title: The ASTRA Initiative: Preparing for future NASA large strategic astrophysics missions
Items.Abstract: This presentation summarizes he Astrophysics Strategic Technology & Research Accelerator (ASTRA) Initiative and discusses, NASA’s progress in executing the Astro2020 Decadal Survey recommendations, and outlines the strategic steps being undertaken to prepare for future strategic astrophysics missions. Support for the community considers previous efforts – including existing concept studies developed for Astro2020, the current global astronomical environment of existing and planned missions, increased industry capability, and technological advances/investments over the past decade. The discussion will highlight the interplay of technological advancements and mission planning essential for future exploration in astrophysics and astronomy and will emphasize the value and criticality of industry and international partnering.

Items.Authors: Janus D. Brink, J. Christopher Clemens, Kieran Leschinski
Items.Title: Pathfinder curved grating spectrometer for the ELT
Items.Abstract: With the Vera C. Rubin observatory on the brink of delivering a flood of transient alerts to the time-domain astronomy community, the need for efficient spectroscopic follow-up is now more critical than ever. We present a compact, high-efficiency curved grating spectrometer design with broad visible band coverage aimed at efficient spectroscopic follow-up. Our pathfinder instrument design is matched to the University of Vienna’s 1.5 m Figl telescope. We describe the spectrometer’s characteristics and expected performance in this configuration and also illustrate the feasibility of extending the design for operation as a visitor instrument of the European Large Telescope.

Items.Authors: Myriam Rodrigues, Alondra Solá, Clément Hottier, Hermine Schnetler, Raziye Artan, Nazim A. Bharmal, Diane Chapuis, Gavin Dalton, Michel Dupieux, Kacem El Hadi, Marc Jaquet, Andreas Kelz, Marie Larrieu, Laurent Martin, Meghna Mohamed, Timothy J. Morris, Ana Perez, Eric Prieto, Jay Stephen, Roser Pello, Mathieu Puech, Thomas Augusteijn, María Luisa García-Vargas, Alessandro Meoli, Ruben Sanchez-Janssen, Christian Surace, Franck Ducret
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: building a comprehensive engineering database
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC, the multi-object spectrograph for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is developed by a dis-  tributed consortium involving multiple institutes and engineering disciplines. Maintaining consistency between  requirements, interfaces, product definitions, verification activities and engineering documentation is therefore a  major systems engineering challenge. To address this, the project implemented a central engineering information  model using ReqSuite® Requirement Management tool. Rather than limiting the repository to requirements  management, the database also stores other engineering artifacts, such as Product Breakdown Structure, inter-  faces, configuration items and verification information, providing a common technical reference for the project.  Behavioural and parametric models -such as observing sequences, funcional analysis and performances calculator-  remain in their specialised engineering tools but are connected to the database through traceability links and  applic

Items.Authors: Angiola Orlando
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: two new Small Aperture Telescopes employing feedhorn-coupled OMT dichroic Kinetic Inductance Detectors
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO) is a ground-based cosmic microwave background (CMB) survey experiment consisting of three 0.5m small-aperture telescopes (SATs) and one 6m large-aperture telescope (LAT), observing from an altitude of 5200m in the Atacama Desert in Chile. These instruments employ over 120000 superconducting transition edge sensor (TES) detectors operating at frequency bands between 30GHz and 280GHz and are conducting regular observations for a broad range of CMB science goals, including searches for primordial gravitational waves through B-mode polarization. We are planning to deploy two additional SATs employing arrays of dual-polarization feedhorn-coupled multichroic Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs) operating at 90/150GHz and bespoke warm detector readout electronics.The integration and testing of both SAT receivers are underway in the UK. We provide an overview of these receivers, discuss integration status and achieved performance on the path to deployment.

Items.Authors: Dinko Milaković, Guido Cupani, Bruce Bassett, Stefano Cristiani, Luca Pasquini
Items.Title: "Perfect" spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph
Items.Abstract: Harperfect is the first application of spectral perfectionism to a high-resolution echelle spectrograph, recon-  structing 1D spectra from 2D detector data via a forward model built on a calibration matrix of PSF shape,  wavelength, and order trace, built entirely from laser frequency comb (LFC) observations. HARPS cannot re-  solve individual LFC lines, so each of 21 148 identified lines directly samples the PSF. We modelled these with  a bivariate Gaussian, determining the PSF anywhere on the detector, calibrating wavelength, and tracing or-  ders more accurately than the standard HARPS pipeline. Applied to 52.5 hours of HARPS data on quasar  HE0515−4414, Harperfect gives S/N comparable to, though slightly lower than, the standard pipeline. Its  value lies in an exact resolution matrix and independent samples, properties standard extraction cannot guar-  antee for a non-separable PSF – a step toward better measurements of fundamental constants and exoplanet  atmospheres.
